message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas

- **The Restorer Rover**
- **Chest Express**
- **Vanity Unit** (a furniture pun)
- **The Dovetail**
- **Sideboard Sid**

## Tomorrow's route

**The only workable order is B → A → C, and it brings the van back at exactly 12:00, with no slack at all.**

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B, done 25 min before the shop opens |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A, inside the 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break near C**, since he has to wait for C anyway |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C, the earliest it will accept |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot, right on the deadline** |

**Why no other order works**
- **Doing A first:** A can't start before 09:00, so the earliest finish is 09:15. Driving 25 minutes to B means arriving at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- **Where C goes:** C can't start before 11:00, so it has to come last.
- **Why 12:00 is the earliest possible return:** C finishes at 11:15 at the earliest, and the drive back takes 45 minutes.

**The risk:** any delay at C makes him late back. That could be a slow reception, unloading that runs past 15 minutes, or traffic on the return. Worth sorting today:
- Ask C whether they'll accept from 10:45. That gives 15 minutes of buffer.
- Or ask whether the 12:00 return can slip a little.
- Or, if neither is possible, move C to another day.

**Departure flexibility:** he can leave as late as about 08:55 and still finish at B by 09:30. Leaving at 08:30 is safer.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Evening-before text (146 characters with the example details filled in)

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Hartley Restoration is due tomorrow between 9:00 and 10:00. Reply or call 01234 567890 if that doesn't suit. Thanks!

- **Keep it to plain characters.** Use straight apostrophes, no emoji, and no long dashes. A single special character can switch the message to a format with a 70-character limit, which would split it into several texts.
- **Watch long names.** A long customer or company name could push it past 160 characters, so check the length when you fill in the details.

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Surfaces and finish:** look for scratches, dents or scuffs picked up in transit, especially on corners and edges.
2. **Moving parts and hardware:** check that doors and drawers open and close properly, and that handles, hinges and feet are secure.
3. **Completeness:** make sure it's the right item and that every part is there, including shelves, keys, glass panels, fittings and any loose pieces.

Ideally, the customer looks over the item with the driver before signing.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed is the better default.** It's easy to store and search, you can attach photos, and the customer can't lose it. The simplest setup is to have customers sign on the driver's phone, with a copy emailed automatically. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer one, or for when the phone or signal fails.

## Proof of delivery

> Proof of delivery is the signed or photographed record showing that the customer received the item, when, and in what condition.
